titleEn: Watch: Could livestock be vaccinated to reduce emissions?
titleZh: 探索通过疫苗减少牲畜甲烷排放的可能性
summaryZh: 爱尔兰国立大学戈尔韦分校的Sinéad Waters博士正开展前沿研究，旨在通过理解反刍动物瘤胃微生物组，开发减少甲烷排放的策略。研究涵盖遗传、饲料添加剂、海藻、3-NOP等，并探讨了通过疫苗刺激动物免疫系统抑制产甲烷菌的设想。相关项目如MAGS和Rumen-Innovate正推动科学成果向农场实践转化，为农业减排提供新路径。
featuredReason: 该新闻聚焦于通过疫苗等前沿生物技术减少牲畜甲烷排放，是智慧畜牧领域在环保与可持续发展方向的重要探索，对理解未来养殖减排技术趋势具有参考价值。
contentFull: Top Stories Beef Dairy Sheep Tillage Machinery Northern Ireland Videos Podcasts Ploughing 2026 Top Stories Beef Dairy Sheep Tillage Machinery Northern Ireland Videos Podcasts Ploughing 2026 Watch: Could livestock be vaccinated to reduce emissions? ![Image 1: Stella Meehan By Stella Meehan September 4, 2026 3:00 PM](https:www.agriland.iefarming-newsauthorstella) Share this article ![Image 2: AI generated](https:www.agriland.iefarming-newswatch-could-livestock-be-vaccinated-to-reduce-emissions) AI generated Could livestock be vaccinated to reduce emissions? This is just one question being explored by scientists in the bid to address climate change and help agriculture reduce its carbon footprint. Dr. Sinéad Waters, principal investigator and lecturer at the University of Galway is involved in ground-breaking research which has the potential to help agriculture address its methane emissions. Her work centres on ruminant microbiomes, with a particular focus on improving productivity while reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. She leads and is involved in a number of research projects looking at methane reduction in Irish beef and dairy farming. Agriland visited Dr. Waters at her laboratory at Univesrity of Galway to find out what farmers need to know about how science is trying to help them - see video below. One of the projects which Dr. Waters is involved in is the MAGS (Methane Abatement in Grazing Systems) project, which is looking at different ways of reducing methane from cattle in Irish grazing systems. This includes looking at genetics, diet, feed additives and manure management. Other research also looked at feed additives and dietary approaches, including seaweeds, fats and 3-NOP, as well as newer technologies such as slow-release supplements and boluses. There is also research into alternative dietary approaches, including the use of rapeseed cake and oil to reduce methane without affecting animal performance. Science in a practical way Dr. Waters grew up on farm and with a deep interest in science, she secured a degree in biotechnology from the University of Galway. She also undertook a PhD around probiotics in conjunction with Alltech and subsequently completed a postdoc at the University of Illinois, before returning to Ireland to work at Teagasc, where she spent almost 20 years. At this time, Dr. Waters also completed a higher diploma in statistics at Trinity College Dublin. Around two years ago, the researcher moved to the University of Galway to become principal investigator, researcher and lecturer in microbiology. "My particular research interest is rumen microbiology or digestive microbiology," she told Agriland. "Looking at that in the context of discovering new methane mitigation strategies for agriculture." The researcher explained that methane production in cattle and sheep is a microbiological process that "we cannot lose sight of". "We need to understand the microbes involved and the biological processes involved in the production of methane gas, so that we can interrupt that process in a way that is not detrimental to the animal or doesn't affect digestive feed or animal health," she said. "By understanding that process we can devise potential strategies, be it... breeding strategies, the feed additives or direct fed microbials, that can reduce that methane production process." Waters explains that research has already led to practical on-farm measures which farmers have adopted to reduce methane emissions. These include feed additives such as Bovaer and others, breeding programmes, which are a little more longer term but are already seeing progress and manure additives which have proven to be successful. Rumen research University of Galway is part of a new European Union research project that will advance sustainable ruminant agriculture through microbiome science. Rumen-Innovate is a consortium including 11 universities and research bodies as well as farming organisations and industry in eight countries across Europe to support the training and development of the next generation of ruminant microbiome scientists. With EU funding of €4.8 million, the project’s focus is on cleaner air, more sustainably produced food, and healthier animals. "Bringing [research projects] together for the life cycle of an animal to see how much methane we can reduce over the lifetime of the animal will be successful in getting proof that they work, giving us insight into the levels of reduction and building these into the national inventory," Dr. Waters explained. She added that methane reduction is possible with various research projects underway, natural attrition of the national herd, the nitrates derogation regulations. Vaccinating for emissions? Dr. Waters has admitted that the suggestion of vaccination in Ireland to help animals produce less methane would be "ideal". "Of course vaccination would be ideal. It would be really good for a country like Ireland or New Zealand, where you could vaccinate your calf or lamb very early in life and the animal is potentially vaccinated with antibodies against methanogens," she said. Basically, a methanogen is a microscopic, single-celled organism that produces methane gas as a by-product of how it gets energy. Potential vaccines could stimulate a cow’s immune system to produce antibodies in its saliva, targeting and suppressing methanogens in the stomach without harming other beneficial gut microbes. Dr. Waters said that there is research ongoing internationally on such an approach which would allow farmers not to have to worry about methane after early life of the animal. Interested in finding out more? This year University of Galway will attend Ploughing 2026 to showcase the ongoing research that is underway at the college. "We're going to be talking about all the projects, MAGS, Rumen Innovate and others and we'd love the public to come in an meet us," Dr. Waters said. There will also be information on agricultural education as well as farm safety, in conjunction with the Ryan Institute. University of Galway will be located at Block 4 Row 10, stand 190 at Ploughing 2026 in Screggan, Co. Offaly from Tuesday, September 15 to Thursday, September 17. translationZh:
牲畜能否通过接种疫苗来减少排放？这是科学家们在应对气候变化、帮助农业降低碳足迹的过程中正在探索的问题之一。

戈尔韦大学的首席研究员兼讲师Sinéad Waters博士参与了一项具有开创性的研究，该研究有望帮助农业解决甲烷排放问题。她的工作聚焦于反刍动物微生物组，特别关注在提高生产力的同时减少温室气体排放。她主持并参与了多个研究项目，旨在减少爱尔兰肉牛和奶牛养殖中的甲烷排放。

Agriland前往戈尔韦大学的实验室拜访了Waters博士，以了解农民需要知道的关于科学如何帮助他们的情况——见下方视频。

Waters博士参与的项目之一是MAGS（放牧系统甲烷减排）项目，该项目正在研究在爱尔兰放牧系统中减少牛甲烷排放的不同方法，包括遗传、日粮、饲料添加剂和粪便管理等方面。

其他研究还涉及饲料添加剂和日粮方案，包括海藻、脂肪和3-NOP，以及缓释补充剂和丸剂等新技术。此外，还有关于替代日粮方案的研究，包括使用菜籽饼和菜籽油在不影响动物性能的情况下减少甲烷。

**科学的实际应用**

Waters博士在农场长大，对科学有浓厚兴趣，她在戈尔韦大学获得了生物技术学位。她还在Alltech公司联合完成了关于益生菌的博士学位，随后在伊利诺伊大学完成了博士后研究，之后回到爱尔兰在Teagasc工作，在那里度过了近20年。在此期间，Waters博士还在都柏林圣三一学院完成了统计学高级文凭。

大约两年前，这位研究员转到戈尔韦大学，成为微生物学的首席研究员、研究者和讲师。

“我的主要研究兴趣是瘤胃微生物学或消化微生物学，”她告诉Agriland，“从发现农业新的甲烷减排策略的角度来研究它。”

这位研究员解释说，牛和羊的甲烷产生是一个微生物过程，“我们不能忽视这一点”。

“我们需要了解参与甲烷气体产生的微生物和生物过程，以便我们能够以对动物无害、不影响消化饲料或动物健康的方式中断这一过程，”她说，“通过了解这一过程，我们可以设计出潜在的策略，无论是育种策略、饲料添加剂还是直接饲喂微生物，都可以减少甲烷的产生过程。”

Waters解释说，研究已经产生了农民可以采用的实用农场措施来减少甲烷排放，包括Bovaer等饲料添加剂、育种计划（虽然更长期，但已初见成效）以及已被证明成功的粪便添加剂。

**瘤胃研究**

戈尔韦大学是欧盟一个新研究项目的成员，该项目将通过微生物组科学推进可持续反刍动物农业。Rumen-Innovate是一个由11所大学和研究机构以及欧洲8个国家的农业组织和行业组成的联盟，旨在支持下一代反刍动物微生物组科学家的培训和发展。

该项目获得欧盟480万欧元的资助，重点是更清洁的空气、更可持续生产的食品和更健康的动物。

“将（研究项目）整合到动物的整个生命周期中，看看在动物一生中能减少多少甲烷，这将成功证明它们的有效性，让我们了解减排水平，并将其纳入国家清单，”Waters博士解释说。

她补充说，通过正在进行的各种研究项目、国家畜群的自然淘汰以及硝酸盐减量法规，甲烷减排是可能的。

**为减排而接种疫苗？**

Waters博士承认，在爱尔兰通过疫苗接种帮助动物减少甲烷产生的建议将是“理想的”。

“当然，疫苗接种将是理想的。这对爱尔兰或新西兰这样的国家来说真的很好，你可以在犊牛或羔羊很小的时候接种疫苗，动物可能接种针对产甲烷菌的抗体，”她说。

基本上，产甲烷菌是一种微小的单细胞生物，在获取能量的过程中会产生甲烷气体作为副产品。

潜在的疫苗可以刺激牛的免疫系统在其唾液中产生抗体，靶向并抑制胃中的产甲烷菌，而不会伤害其他有益的肠道微生物。

Waters博士说，国际上正在进行关于这种方法的研究，这将使农民在动物早期生活后不必担心甲烷问题。

**想了解更多？**

今年，戈尔韦大学将参加Ploughing 2026，展示该大学正在进行的研究。

“我们将讨论所有项目，如MAGS、Rumen-Innovate等，我们欢迎公众来与我们交流，”Waters博士说。

还将提供农业教育以及农场安全方面的信息，与Ryan研究所合作。

戈尔韦大学将位于Ploughing 2026的Block 4 Row 10，展位190，地点在Offaly郡Screggan，时间为9月15日（星期二）至9月17日（星期四）。
